diagnostic.title: AI Essentials Placement Diagnostic
diagnostic.description: Ten quick questions that help the course start at the right place for you.

items.prompt: A tool cuts the time a task takes from two hours to ten minutes. What usually happens next in real workplaces?
options: People do more of that kind of work, not less
items.explanation: When something gets cheap, people use more of it. That's Jevons paradox, and it's why "AI does this faster" rarely means "there's nothing left to do."

items.prompt: Which is most likely to be replaced first by AI?
options: The routine parts inside a job

items.prompt: An AI writes a confident paragraph with a specific date, name, and number in it. What does that confidence tell you?
options: Very little — confident wording and correct facts are separate things

items.prompt: Where does a language model's "knowledge" come from?
options: Patterns in a large pile of text it was trained on

items.prompt: Your first prompt gives you a mediocre answer. What's the best next move?
options: Add much more text to the prompt
Change one thing, then see what that changed

items.prompt: You want AI to summarize a document you have. What matters most?
You need to sort 500 emails into three simple categories, every day. Which is the better fit?
options: The largest, most capable model available
Any model — it makes no difference

items.prompt: You want to hand an AI a photo of a handwritten receipt and get the total back. What kind of model do you need?
options: One that accepts images as well as text
A larger version of a text-only model
items.explanation: Models that take more than text — images, audio, video — are called multimodal. Text-only models can't see your receipt no matter how large they are.

items.prompt: You build something that drafts replies to customer questions and sends them automatically. What's the most important thing to add?
options: A person who checks before anything goes out

items.prompt: Your automation works on the ten cases you tested. What's the risk when it meets a case you didn't test?
options: It produces something wrong and doesn't flag it
It asks you what to do

milestones.name: Pick it
milestones.objective: Decide what you're going to automate, and decide what "finished" looks like before you start.
milestones.completion: At the end, the learner has one sentence naming the task, who it's for, and how they'll know it worked.
checkInPrompts: What's the task, and how often do you do it now?
Who benefits when this works — you, or someone else?
How will you know it's done? Not "it's good," but something you could actually check.
milestones.authorNote: The most common failure here is over-scoping. Talk learners down, not up. A project abandoned on day four teaches nothing.

milestones.name: Make it work once
milestones.objective: Get a version that produces the right output one time, on one real example. It does not need to be repeatable yet.
milestones.completion: At the end, the learner has one real output they'd actually use, plus the prompt or setup that produced it.
checkInPrompts: Show me what it produced. Would you actually use this?
What did you have to give it before it worked?
What did you try first that didn't work?

milestones.name: Fix what's broken
milestones.objective: Run it on cases you haven't tried yet. Find where it fails, and decide which failures matter.
milestones.completion: At the end, the learner has three cases they ran, what went wrong in at least one, and what they changed.
checkInPrompts: What did it get wrong? Be specific.
Did it ever make something up that looked correct?
Which failures can you live with, and which would stop you from using this?
milestones.authorNote: This is where hallucinations stop being abstract. Learners see it happen to their own work, which is why the lesson sits here rather than in week one.

milestones.name: Make it run again without you rebuilding it
milestones.objective: The test that defines this course: can you run this next week without starting over?
milestones.completion: At the end, the learner has a saved prompt and checklist, a script someone can run, or something that fires on a schedule. Any of the three counts.
checkInPrompts: If you did this again next Tuesday, what would you have to redo?
What did you save, and where is it?
Could someone else run this from what you wrote down?
milestones.authorNote: This repeats the project-selection question against the real thing. A saved prompt, template, and checklist genuinely count. Requiring unattended automation would fail most learners on free-tier tools.

milestones.name: Ship it and say what you learned
milestones.objective: Use it for real, then say plainly what the AI did, what you did, and where you'd tell someone to be careful.
milestones.completion: At the end, the learner has a short write-up and, optionally, a screenshot or link to the thing they made.
checkInPrompts: What does the AI handle, and what do you still have to check yourself?
Where would this hurt someone if it got something wrong and nobody noticed?
What would you tell someone starting this from scratch?
milestones.authorNote: The ethics content lands here rather than in a standalone unit. It's hardest to teach abstractly and easiest to teach to someone holding something they built.
